title: A hash table from scratch
body: A hash table stores each key in a bucket chosen by a hash function. Looking a key up means hashing it, picking the bucket and searching the few entries there, which is constant time when buckets stay short. This version keeps an array of association lists (separate chaining), so a collision just means two entries share a bucket.

The *load factor* is the number of entries divided by the number of buckets. When it exceeds a threshold the table doubles its bucket array and re-inserts everything, which keeps buckets short. Because every doubling touches all entries but happens after the number of entries has doubled, the cost per insertion is constant on average (amortised).

State the representation invariant and check it: every entry lives in the bucket its key hashes to, the stored size equals the number of entries, and no key appears twice. The mutable table is easy to corrupt with a missed update, so a `rep_ok` function that verifies these facts is cheap insurance in tests.
challenge: Add `remove t k` to the table that deletes a key if present and keeps `size` correct, then remove key 42 and print the length and whether `find_opt` still finds it.
question: Why does doubling the bucket array keep insertion constant time on average?
correct: Each doubling costs time proportional to the entries, but it only happens after the entry count has doubled
wrong: Because the array is copied without looking at entries
reasoning: The expensive resizes are rare enough that their total cost, spread over all insertions, is a constant per insertion.

title: Amortised analysis with a two-list queue
body: A single operation can be slow while a long sequence of them is cheap. The two-list queue pushes onto a back list in constant time and pops from a front list; when the front is empty it reverses the back, which costs the length of the back. One pop can cost a lot, but each element is moved from back to front at most once in its lifetime.

The *banker's method* makes this precise: charge each push a few units, spend one to pay for the push and save the rest to pay in advance for the single reversal move that element will need later. The total cost of any sequence of n operations is then at most a constant times n, so the *amortised* cost per operation is constant. The code counts real units so you can watch the bound hold.

Amortised bounds assume each version of the structure is used once. If you keep an old version and pop from it repeatedly, every pop pays the full reversal again, and the bound collapses. Persistent data structures need laziness to restore amortisation, which is why the next lessons on streams and memoisation matter.
expectedStdout:
popped 1000, total cost 3001 for 2001 operations
amortised cost at most 3 per operation: true
reusing one version costs 1001000 for 1000 pops
challenge: Run 10 pushes followed by 10 pops with the counting queue and print the total cost, which should be 30 (10 pushes, 10 pops and 10 moved elements).
question: What does the amortised bound assume about how the queue is used?
correct: Each version is used once; reusing an old version repeats the expensive reversal
wrong: That the queue never holds more than ten elements
That pops always happen before pushes
reasoning: The saved credit from each push is spent exactly once, so reusing a version lets the same credit be spent again and the accounting fails.

title: Red-black trees: balance by colour
body: A red-black tree is a binary search tree whose nodes are coloured so the tree stays roughly balanced. Two invariants do the work: no red node has a red child, and every path from the root to a leaf passes through the same number of black nodes. Together they bound the height by about twice the logarithm of the size, so lookup and insertion are logarithmic even for sorted input.

Okasaki's insertion is short. Insert as in an ordinary tree, colouring the new node red, then rebalance on the way back up. Whenever a black node has a red child with a red child (four possible shapes), one `balance` rewrite turns that shape into a red parent with two black children. The root is finally made black, which restores the invariant.

The four shapes share one result, which an or-pattern expresses directly. Because the invariants are easy to state, write a checker for them and run it after every insertion in a test: a missed shape in `balance` shows up as a violated invariant long before it shows up as a slow tree.
code:
type color = R | B
type 'a t = E | T of color * 'a t * 'a * 'a t

let balance = function
  | B, T (R, T (R, a, x, b), y, c), z, d
  | B, T (R, a, x, T (R, b, y, c)), z, d
  | B, a, x, T (R, T (R, b, y, c), z, d)
  | B, a, x, T (R, b, y, T (R, c, z, d)) ->
      T (R, T (B, a, x, b), y, T (B, c, z, d))
  | color, a, x, b -> T (color, a, x, b)

let insert x s =
  let rec ins = function
    | E -> T (R, E, x, E)
    | T (color, a, y, b) as t ->
        if x < y then balance (color, ins a, y, b)
        else if x > y then balance (color, a, y, ins b)
        else t
  in
  match ins s with T (_, a, y, b) -> T (B, a, y, b) | E -> assert false

let rec size = function E -> 0 | T (_, a, _, b) -> size a + 1 + size b
let rec height = function E -> 0 | T (_, a, _, b) -> 1 + max (height a) (height b)
let rec to_list = function E -> [] | T (_, a, x, b) -> to_list a @ [ x ] @ to_list b

(* Black height of a tree, or None if the invariants are violated. *)
let rec black_height = function
  | E -> Some 1
  | T (color, a, _, b) -> (
      let bad_red = function T (R, _, _, _) -> color = R | _ -> false in
      if bad_red a || bad_red b then None
      else
        match (black_height a, black_height b) with
        | Some x, Some y when x = y -> Some (if color = B then x + 1 else x)
        | _ -> None)

let () =
  let t = List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) E (List.init 1000 (fun i -> i + 1)) in
  Printf.printf "size %d\n" (size t);
  Printf.printf "sorted: %b\n" (to_list t = List.init 1000 (fun i -> i + 1));
  Printf.printf "invariants hold: %b\n" (black_height t <> None);
  Printf.printf "height at most 20 for 1000 sorted keys: %b\n" (height t <= 20)
expectedStdout:
size 1000
sorted: true
invariants hold: true
height at most 20 for 1000 sorted keys: true
challenge: Write `mem x t` for the red-black tree and print whether it finds 500 and 1001 in a tree built from the keys 1 to 1000.
solution:
type color = R | B
type 'a t = E | T of color * 'a t * 'a * 'a t

let balance = function
  | B, T (R, T (R, a, x, b), y, c), z, d
  | B, T (R, a, x, T (R, b, y, c)), z, d
  | B, a, x, T (R, T (R, b, y, c), z, d)
  | B, a, x, T (R, b, y, T (R, c, z, d)) ->
      T (R, T (B, a, x, b), y, T (B, c, z, d))
  | color, a, x, b -> T (color, a, x, b)

let insert x s =
  let rec ins = function
    | E -> T (R, E, x, E)
    | T (color, a, y, b) as t ->
        if x < y then balance (color, ins a, y, b)
        else if x > y then balance (color, a, y, ins b)
        else t
  in
  match ins s with T (_, a, y, b) -> T (B, a, y, b) | E -> assert false

let rec mem x = function
  | E -> false
  | T (_, a, y, b) -> if x < y then mem x a else if x > y then mem x b else true

let () =
  let t = List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) E (List.init 1000 (fun i -> i + 1)) in
  Printf.printf "%b %b\n" (mem 500 t) (mem 1001 t)
question: Which two invariants keep a red-black tree balanced?
correct: No red node has a red child, and every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes
wrong: Every node has exactly two children, and keys are unique
Red nodes are always on the left, and black nodes on the right
reasoning: Equal black height fixes the shortest path length and the no-red-red rule limits how much longer any path can be, so the height is at most about twice the minimum.

title: Lazy streams and the sieve of Eratosthenes
body: A stream is a list whose tail is computed on demand, so it can be infinite. `type 'a stream = Cons of 'a * 'a stream Lazy.t` pairs a head with a lazy tail. Nothing past the head exists until someone forces it, and forcing happens at most once because `Lazy` caches the result.

Streams make some algorithms read like their mathematical definitions. The sieve of Eratosthenes is 'take the first number, keep only the numbers not divisible by it, and sieve the rest', and Fibonacci numbers are 'two numbers and then the stream that follows'. You take as many elements as you need with a `take` function and leave the infinite remainder unevaluated.

The standard library provides the same idea as `Seq`, whose tails are functions rather than cached lazy values, so a `Seq` recomputes work each time it is traversed. Prefer `Seq` for one-pass pipelines and a memoising stream when the same elements are demanded many times, and remember that a stream holding onto its head keeps every forced element alive.
challenge: Define the stream of powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) with a function like `fibs`, and print its first eight elements.
question: Why does forcing a lazy value twice evaluate its body only once?
correct: Lazy caches the result of the first force
wrong: Because the second force raises an exception
Because lazy values cannot be forced twice
reasoning: A lazy value stores its result after the first evaluation, which is what makes streams safe to share.

title: Memoisation and dynamic programming
body: Memoisation remembers the result of a function for each argument it has seen, so repeated calls become lookups. The naive Fibonacci recomputes the same subproblems exponentially many times; with a table the number of real computations is linear. This works whenever the function is *pure*, because returning a stored answer is indistinguishable from recomputing it.

A recursive function cannot be memoised by wrapping it from outside, because its recursive calls still go to the unmemoised version. Write it in *open recursion* style, taking `self` as a parameter for its recursive calls, and tie the knot with a `memo_rec` that supplies a table-checking `self`. The same trick turns a clear recursive definition into dynamic programming without rewriting it as loops.

Dynamic programming is memoisation of overlapping subproblems. Edit distance between two strings is the classic example: the distance of two prefixes depends only on the distances of shorter prefixes, so a table indexed by the two lengths holds all the work. Count how many table entries are computed to see the saving.
expectedStdout:
6765 with 21891 calls
6765 with 21 calls
edit distance 3 from 56 table entries
challenge: Use `memo_rec` to count the number of ways to climb 30 stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time (ways n = ways (n-1) + ways (n-2), with ways 0 = ways 1 = 1) and print it.
question: Why must a recursive function be written in open-recursion style to be memoised?
correct: Its recursive calls must go through the memoising wrapper, which a plain recursive reference would bypass
wrong: Because Hashtbl cannot store recursive values
Because open recursion makes the function faster by itself
reasoning: Passing self lets the memoising wrapper intercept every recursive call, so each distinct argument is computed once.

title: Persistent arrays as balanced trees
body: An ordinary array is mutable: updating it destroys the old version. A persistent array keeps every version usable. The simplest design stores the elements at the leaves of a balanced binary tree; reading index i walks down choosing left or right by comparing i with the midpoint, and writing index i rebuilds only the path from the root to that leaf while sharing every other subtree.

Both operations take time logarithmic in the length, not constant, and an update allocates a handful of nodes instead of copying the whole array. This is the price of persistence: you pay a log factor to keep old versions, in exchange for undo, backtracking and safe sharing between threads with no locks.

You can observe the sharing directly. After setting one element, the subtree that did not contain it is the very same block in memory, which physical equality `==` confirms. Use persistent arrays when you need history; if you only ever use the newest version, a plain mutable array is simpler and faster.
expectedStdout:
9 100
untouched elements agree: true
right half shared by all versions: true
versions all usable: 1 1 -1
challenge: Write `to_list a` that returns the elements of a persistent array in order, and print it for the array of squares of 0 to 5 after setting index 2 to 0.
question: What does an update of a persistent tree-array allocate?
correct: New nodes only along the path to the changed leaf; every other subtree is shared
wrong: A complete copy of the array
Nothing, because it mutates in place
reasoning: Path copying rebuilds just the ancestors of the changed leaf, so the old and new versions share everything else.

title: 2-3 trees: balance without colours
body: A 2-3 tree is a search tree whose nodes hold one key and two children (a 2-node) or two keys and three children (a 3-node), with every leaf at the same depth. Because the leaves are all at the same depth, the tree is perfectly balanced, and lookup follows one path of logarithmic length.

Insertion goes down to a leaf and comes back up. A 2-node that receives a key becomes a 3-node, and a 3-node that receives a key *splits* into a 2-node on each side and pushes the middle key up to its parent. A split that reaches the root creates a new root, which is the only way the tree grows taller, so all leaves stay at the same depth.

The recursive insert returns either `Fit` (the subtree absorbed the key) or `Split (left, middle, right)` (the parent must absorb a middle key). Red-black trees encode balanced trees with colours: the *left-leaning* variant encodes 2-3 trees exactly, while the four-case version in the previous lesson corresponds to 2-3-4 trees, whose full nodes hold three keys, which is why it needs four rewrite shapes. The idea of splitting a full node and pushing the middle key up is the same in both. The checker below verifies equal leaf depth and sorted order.
code:
type 'a t = E | N2 of 'a t * 'a * 'a t | N3 of 'a t * 'a * 'a t * 'a * 'a t
type 'a ins = Fit of 'a t | Split of 'a t * 'a * 'a t

let rec ins x = function
  | E -> Split (E, x, E)
  | N2 (l, y, r) as t ->
      if x = y then Fit t
      else if x < y then (
        match ins x l with
        | Fit l' -> Fit (N2 (l', y, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Fit (N3 (a, z, b, y, r)))
      else (
        match ins x r with
        | Fit r' -> Fit (N2 (l, y, r'))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Fit (N3 (l, y, a, z, b)))
  | N3 (l, y, m, w, r) as t ->
      if x = y || x = w then Fit t
      else if x < y then (
        match ins x l with
        | Fit l' -> Fit (N3 (l', y, m, w, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (a, z, b), y, N2 (m, w, r)))
      else if x < w then (
        match ins x m with
        | Fit m' -> Fit (N3 (l, y, m', w, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (l, y, a), z, N2 (b, w, r)))
      else (
        match ins x r with
        | Fit r' -> Fit (N3 (l, y, m, w, r'))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (l, y, m), w, N2 (a, z, b)))

let insert x t = match ins x t with Fit t' -> t' | Split (a, z, b) -> N2 (a, z, b)

let rec to_list = function
  | E -> []
  | N2 (l, x, r) -> to_list l @ [ x ] @ to_list r
  | N3 (l, x, m, y, r) -> to_list l @ [ x ] @ to_list m @ [ y ] @ to_list r

(* Depth of all leaves, or None if they are not all at the same depth. *)
let rec depth = function
  | E -> Some 0
  | N2 (l, _, r) -> (match (depth l, depth r) with Some a, Some b when a = b -> Some (a + 1) | _ -> None)
  | N3 (l, _, m, _, r) ->
      (match (depth l, depth m, depth r) with Some a, Some b, Some c when a = b && b = c -> Some (a + 1) | _ -> None)

let () =
  (* 997 is prime, so multiplying by 389 mod 997 visits 500 distinct keys in a scrambled order *)
  let keys = List.init 500 (fun i -> (i * 389 + 1) mod 997) in
  let t = List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) E keys in
  Printf.printf "sorted: %b\n" (to_list t = List.sort_uniq compare keys);
  Printf.printf "all leaves at the same depth: %b\n" (depth t <> None);
  Printf.printf "keys: %d\n" (List.length (to_list t));
  Printf.printf "height at most 9: %b\n" (match depth t with Some d -> d <= 9 | None -> false)
expectedStdout:
sorted: true
all leaves at the same depth: true
keys: 500
height at most 9: true
challenge: Insert the keys 1 to 7 into an empty tree in order and print the depth of the result.
solution:
type 'a t = E | N2 of 'a t * 'a * 'a t | N3 of 'a t * 'a * 'a t * 'a * 'a t
type 'a ins = Fit of 'a t | Split of 'a t * 'a * 'a t

let rec ins x = function
  | E -> Split (E, x, E)
  | N2 (l, y, r) as t ->
      if x = y then Fit t
      else if x < y then (
        match ins x l with
        | Fit l' -> Fit (N2 (l', y, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Fit (N3 (a, z, b, y, r)))
      else (
        match ins x r with
        | Fit r' -> Fit (N2 (l, y, r'))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Fit (N3 (l, y, a, z, b)))
  | N3 (l, y, m, w, r) as t ->
      if x = y || x = w then Fit t
      else if x < y then (
        match ins x l with
        | Fit l' -> Fit (N3 (l', y, m, w, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (a, z, b), y, N2 (m, w, r)))
      else if x < w then (
        match ins x m with
        | Fit m' -> Fit (N3 (l, y, m', w, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (l, y, a), z, N2 (b, w, r)))
      else (
        match ins x r with
        | Fit r' -> Fit (N3 (l, y, m, w, r'))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (l, y, m), w, N2 (a, z, b)))

let insert x t = match ins x t with Fit t' -> t' | Split (a, z, b) -> N2 (a, z, b)

let rec depth = function
  | E -> 0
  | N2 (l, _, _) -> 1 + depth l
  | N3 (l, _, _, _, _) -> 1 + depth l

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (depth (List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) E [ 1; 2; 3; 4; 5; 6; 7 ]))
question: How does a 2-3 tree grow taller?
correct: Only when a split reaches the root and a new root is created, so all leaves stay at the same depth
wrong: By adding a new leaf below the deepest existing leaf
By recolouring nodes until the tree is balanced
reasoning: Every other insertion is absorbed below the root, so the depth of all leaves increases together or not at all.
